findings.problem: role_duties[1] tells the transferring pharmacy to "complete the federal voiding and transfer records for a Schedule III-V refill transfer" but the section never says what those records are, and forms_records is empty.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(b)(2) requires the transferring pharmacist to write VOID on the face of the invalidated prescription (or annotate the electronic record), to record on the reverse the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number and the receiving pharmacist's name, and to record the date of transfer and the transferring pharmacist's name; 1306.25(b)(3) requires the receiving pharmacist to write "transfer" on the face and to reduce to writing the original issue date, the original number of refills authorized, the date of original dispensing, the number of valid refills remaining with dates and locations of previous refills, and both pharmacies' identifying data; 1306.25(c) requires both prescriptions to be kept two years from the date of last refill. A candidate who accepts the section's instruction has no way to execute it. This is recorded as advisory rather than as a criterion failure because the section's declared subtopic is "Refill and transfer limits" and none of its five learning objectives claims to teach transfer recordkeeping content.

findings.problem: The initial-dispensing electronic transfer is described as one-time and reaching Schedules II-V, but the section never states what happens to authorized refills that travel with such a transfer.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) has a second sentence the section omits: if the transferred prescription is for a Schedule III, IV or V substance and includes authorized refills, the refills are transferred with the initial prescription to the receiving pharmacy. Learning objective 5 promises to "separate the initial-dispensing electronic transfer from the refill-purpose transfer", so a candidate asked whether Pharmacy B may dispense the remaining refills on a never-dispensed electronic Schedule IV prescription it received under 1306.08(e) is answering inside the section's declared scope. Nothing in the section states the wrong rule, and exceptions[0] ("a transfer does not create new refill authority") does not contradict 1306.08(e), so this is an omission rather than a distortion.

findings.problem: Both federal transfer pathways are stated without noting that each is expressly conditioned on state law permitting the transfer.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(e) makes the refill-purpose transfer procedure "permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law", and 21 CFR 1306.08(g) says the same of the initial-dispensing electronic transfer. On a state-law examination the conditional character of the federal permission is the point of contact between the two bodies of law. The section is not wrong: 247 CMR 9.14(1) affirmatively requires Massachusetts pharmacies to transfer on patient request, so the state-law condition is satisfied here and the section reaches the correct operative result.

results.summary: Publishable as written. I read every controlling provision rather than the rule summaries. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) says exactly what quick_review[0] says - no Schedule III or IV prescription filled or refilled more than six months after the issue date, no more than five refills - and 1306.22(e)(4) confirms the section's claim that only a new and separate prescription lifts either limit. 247 CMR 9.04(13) reads "A licensee may not fill or refill a prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance more than six months after the date on which said prescription was issued. A prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance may not be refilled more than five times", which vindicates the section's insistence in common_traps[5] that the six-month bar reaches the first fill and not only refills; 247 CMR 9.04(15) does exclude institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(13), and the section's careful hedge "through this provision" in decision_logic[2] is right, because the exclusion removes the state subsection and not any other law. 247 CMR 9.14 reads as the section states it, clause by clause: (1) a pharmacy shall transfer at the request of the patient or agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, (2) the pharmacy may act as the patient's agent, (3) no transfer fee, (4)(a) Schedule VI transfers in the same manner as Schedules III-V, (4)(b) up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, (4)(c) no transfer of a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription more than one year from issue. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) confirms the one-time limit and the real-time shared-database alternative, and 1306.25(b)(1) confirms the pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement; 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) confirms that a certified pharmacy technician may perform transfers "for prescriptions issued for controlled substances in Schedule VI only" with the approval of the pharmacist on duty. 21 CFR 1306.08(e)-(g) confirms the separate one-time initial-dispensing electronic pathway for Schedules II-V between retail pharmacies at the patient's request, with no shared-database counterpart, so exceptions[3] and common_traps[3] are both sound. I paid particular attention to the interaction defects this section could have had and did not find them. The federal one-time refill-transfer limit and the Massachusetts duty to transfer on request are not left sitting in separate fields: decision_logic[4] sequences them (check the one-time limit before applying the state duty), ma_vs_federal[0] states that the federal limits remain operative under the state rules, and common_traps[2] names the exact error of reading the state duty as displacing the federal cap. The reasoning in ma_vs_federal[1] for why the federal one-time limit does not reach Schedule VI is correct on the authorities: 105 CMR 700.002(F) defines Schedule VI as all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule, and Massachusetts Schedules II-V incorporate 21 CFR 1308.12-1308.15 by reference, so a Schedule VI drug is outside the federal schedules that 1306.25 reaches. The six-month figures are each tied to a named schedule and authority and the one-year Schedule VI transfer ceiling is stated separately, so no figure is left free to migrate between schedules. Practice mapping passes. MA-Q-0120 and MA-Q-0397 are both RELEASED. MA-Q-0120 turns on 9.14(1), 9.14(3), 9.14(4)(a)-(c) and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d), and every one of those propositions is taught in quick_review[2], ma_vs_federal[1]-[2], role_duties[3] and timing_deadlines[2]; its distractor E, which invites the candidate to carry a six-month figure to a ten-month-old Schedule VI prescription, is defeated by timing_deadlines[2]. MA-Q-0397 turns on the fee prohibition and the agency permission, both stated in quick_review[2] and role_duties[1]. Three Low advisory findings are recorded: the transfer recordkeeping asserted in role_duties[1] is never given content and forms_records is empty; the second sentence of 21 CFR 1306.08(e), under which authorized refills travel with an initial-dispensing electronic transfer, is omitted; and the state-law condition in 1306.25(e) and 1306.08(g) is not stated. None of these would lead a candidate to the wrong answer or to unlawful conduct in Massachusetts, so they do not defeat any criterion.

findings.location: forms_records (all three entries); role_duties[0]; exceptions[0]; decision_logic[1]; common_traps[0]
findings.problem: The section instructs the candidate four separate times to validate the "required prescription elements" that the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception does not remove, and declares in learning_objectives[1] that the candidate will "Apply Massachusetts prescription elements", but it never states what those elements are. forms_records covers only the oral reduction to writing, the customer identifier and the written-form requirement.
findings.rationale: The controlling lists are short, concrete and testable. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) requires a written or electronic prescription to state the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date of delivery, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the name and address of the patient except in a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any required cautionary statements, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. 105 CMR 721.020(D) adds the quantity of dosage units and, for a Schedule II opioid, the partial-fill notation, and 105 CMR 721.020(C) requires the practitioner's name and address to be clearly indicated. The section links MA-Q-0118, whose correct answer is that patient identification and directions for use are both required elements that must be resolved before dispensing; the section carries MA-RX-REQUIRED-ELEMENTS as a declared dependency and cites it in four places, yet a candidate studying only this section cannot say which fields are mandatory. Telling a reader to validate a list without supplying the list is a defect in the section's own terms, not merely less detail than the regulation.

findings.problem: The section tells the candidate that a designated additional drug is "reportable to the prescription monitoring program" but never gives the reporting deadline, and timing_deadlines carries only the two one-year clocks.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires the dispensing information to be transmitted to the Department or its agent by the end of the next business day, covering all controlled substances dispensed since the previous transmission. learning_objectives[2] promises the candidate will apply "the additional-drug consequences", and the reporting window is one of them. This is recorded as Low because the two deadlines the section does state - the 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) one-year transfer bar and the 247 CMR 9.04(12) one-year validity limit - are both accurate and are the deadlines that decide Schedule VI questions, and because nothing in the section states a wrong period.

findings.problem: The section presents the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception without mentioning the Failover, which 105 CMR 721.010 defines exclusively in terms of Schedule VI.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.010 defines a Failover as "a document that originates as a schedule VI Electronic Prescription, but experiences an unforeseen defect ... during Electronic Transmission, and is converted to a computer generated facsimile", and 105 CMR 721.020(G) then treats a qualifying Failover as an oral prescription requiring no written or electronic follow-up. The Failover is therefore a Schedule VI device by definition and belongs, at least by cross-reference, in the Schedule VI section. Its absence here is what leaves the sibling section SG-MA-ORAL-PRESCRIPTIONS free to teach the Failover with no schedule limit at all, which is the High finding recorded against that section. Judged on its own, this section states no wrong proposition about the exception it does teach, so the omission is Low here.

results.summary: One edit-sized gap in an otherwise accurate and unusually well-disciplined section. Every substantive proposition I checked against the official text held. 105 CMR 700.002(F) reads "Schedule VI shall consist of all prescription drugs, which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner", which is quick_review[0]. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) does except "Prescriptions issued for controlled substances in schedule VI" from the electronic-prescribing requirement, and the proviso opening 721.070(A) - that no written or oral prescription may be issued under an exception in an effort to circumvent the electronic requirement - supports the section's repeated insistence that the exception removes only the format mandate. 247 CMR 9.04(12) reads exactly as quick_review[3] and exceptions[1] state it, including the professional-judgment continuation of a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging where the prescription has expired or has no refills left and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner. I checked the three hardest points in this section and all three are right. First, exceptions[2]: 247 CMR 9.04(15) reads "The requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(4), (5), (6), (9), (10), (12), (13), and (14) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies", so the section's claim that the Schedule VI validity clock, the day-counting convention and the customer-identifier duty all fall away for that facility type is correct and correctly scoped. Second, common_traps[2]: the one-year transfer bar in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) and the one-year validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12) really are two distinct provisions that happen to share a figure, and the section refuses to restate either as the other - this is precisely the kind of collision that usually goes wrong and here it does not. Third, exceptions[3]: 247 CMR 9.04(10) requires the pharmacist to count the day after the prescription was written as day one, and the section correctly composes that with the one-year Schedule VI clock instead of leaving the two facts unconnected. The additional-drug chain also verifies end to end: 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a Schedule VI controlled substance the Department determines carries a bona fide potential for abuse, 700.012(C)(8) gives the Commissioner's determination factors and the duty to notify all dispensers that they must begin reporting, 700.012(A)(1) makes the dispensing reportable, and 247 CMR 9.04(14)(b) requires a customer identifier for a controlled substance classified as an additional drug under 700.012(A)(1) - with the hardship route in 9.04(14)(c) conditioned on a documented reason plus the recipient's printed name and address and signature, as forms_records[1] says. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) confirms the "Schedule VI only" limit on certified-technician transfers, so common_traps[4] is right to rest on the word only. 105 CMR 721.020(F) confirms forms_records[2]: a written prescription must be on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements, and 105 CMR 721.040(A) makes a non-conforming format invalid and unfillable. The failure is narrower than any of that. The section instructs the candidate four times to validate the "required prescription elements" that the Schedule VI exception does not remove, and promises in learning_objectives[1] to teach the candidate to apply Massachusetts prescription elements, but never states them, while linking MA-Q-0118, whose answer is that patient identification and directions for use are both mandatory. Supplying the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) and 105 CMR 721.020(D) list in forms_records closes it. Practice mapping nonetheless passes: MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0118 and MA-Q-0120 are all RELEASED, and the proposition each one actually turns on - that the Schedule VI follow-up exception is not a validity waiver, that Schedule VI status confers no exemption from prescription content, and the 247 CMR 9.14 transfer framework with the certified-technician provision - is taught here.

findings.problem: The section teaches the Failover as a general no-follow-up route for any oral prescription arising from a transmission failure. It never states the definitional limit that a Failover is a Schedule VI prescription, so a candidate following decision_logic[3] will waive a statutory follow-up duty on a Schedule II-V oral prescription taken during an electronic-prescribing outage.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.010 defines Failover as "a document that originates as a schedule VI Electronic Prescription, but experiences an unforeseen defect, as outlined in Department guidance, during Electronic Transmission, and is converted to a computer generated facsimile". Only such a document can be treated under 105 CMR 721.020(G) as an oral prescription needing no written or electronic follow-up. decision_logic[3] instead keys the Failover to the condition "A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission", which is the language of a different provision - 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2), the ePrescribing exception for circumstances where electronic prescribing is not available due to temporary technological or electrical failure. A prescription issued under 721.070(A)(2) is not a Failover; it is an ordinary written or oral prescription issued under an exception, and if it is an oral prescription for a controlled substance in Schedules II through V then 105 CMR 721.070(B) obliges the practitioner to cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy within not more than seven business days, with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) imposing its own follow-up duty as well. The section's three-condition checklist in exceptions[2] and common_traps[4] reproduces 721.020(G)(1)-(3) faithfully but omits the gate that actually separates the two situations, so the checklist reads as complete when it is not - a Schedule IV oral prescription taken during an outage satisfies all three of the stated conditions and would be wrongly classified as a Failover. The consequence is not an examination slip alone: the pharmacy would record no expectation of a follow-up prescription the law requires the prescriber to deliver.

findings.problem: The condition and the action in decision_logic[3] belong to two different provisions, so the branch fires on facts that do not satisfy the rule it applies.
findings.rationale: The condition is "A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission", which is 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2). The action is "Treat a qualifying Failover as an oral prescription needing no follow-up", which is 105 CMR 721.020(G) and reaches only a document that, under the 105 CMR 721.010 definition, originated as a Schedule VI electronic prescription and was converted to a computer generated facsimile. A decision branch is only useful if its condition selects the cases its action governs; this one does not, and the three checks the action names do not correct it because a Schedule II-V oral prescription taken during an outage passes all three. The repair is to make the condition read on the definition - an electronic Schedule VI prescription that failed in transmission and arrived as a computer generated facsimile - and to add a sibling branch routing a Schedule II-V oral prescription issued under 721.070(A) to the 721.070(B) follow-up duty.

findings.problem: A Schedule VI-only device is stated in unrestricted terms three times, and the trap written to guard it names the wrong guard.
findings.rationale: quick_review[4] says "A Failover counts as an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up, but only where all three of its conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug", exceptions[2] repeats that the three conditions are conjunctive, and common_traps[4] warns that "Calling any transmission failure a Failover skips the conditions". Each sentence tells the candidate that the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)(1)-(3) are the whole of the qualification. They are not; the schedule limit sits in the definition at 105 CMR 721.010, upstream of those conditions. Stating a limited rule three times in unlimited terms, and then supplying a checklist that appears exhaustive, is a stronger invitation to overgeneralize than silence would have been. The additional-drug condition the section does state is in fact a further narrowing within Schedule VI, since 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a Schedule VI controlled substance the Department has determined carries a bona fide potential for abuse - a candidate could reasonably read that condition as implying the rule otherwise reaches all schedules.

findings.location: decision_logic[3] read together with quick_review[4], exceptions[2] and common_traps[4]
findings.problem: Taken as a study unit, the Failover material would change what a pharmacist does at the counter, not merely how a candidate answers.
findings.rationale: A pharmacist who has studied this section, takes a telephoned Schedule IV prescription during an electronic-prescribing outage, and applies decision_logic[3] will record the prescription as needing no follow-up. In fact 105 CMR 721.070(B) obliges the prescriber to cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than seven business days, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) imposes its own follow-up duty, with s. 20(c) directing that violations be reported to the prescriber's licensing board and to the commissioner or the Board of Registration in Pharmacy. The pharmacy would neither expect nor chase a document the law requires, and the prescription file would stand incomplete. That is the difference between a section that is thin and a section that distorts, and it is why this criterion fails rather than merely the exceptions criterion.

findings.problem: The section makes the seven-day written follow-up route available only where the prescriber personally "holds" an electronic-prescribing exception, and instructs the candidate in decision_logic[1] that a prescriber who "holds no electronic-prescribing exception" owes an electronic follow-up within two days. Most Massachusetts electronic-prescribing exceptions are not held by a practitioner at all.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish exceptions by regulation and limits them to seven categories, only one of which - clause (iii), the time-limited waiver process for practitioners demonstrating economic hardship or technological limitations - is a waiver a practitioner applies for and holds. The implementing list at 105 CMR 721.070(A) is likewise category-based: veterinarians, temporary technological or electrical failure, emergency situations, prescriptions that cannot be issued electronically under law, prescriptions issued outside the jurisdiction, expedited partner therapy, compounded preparations, Schedule VI, durable medical equipment, certain long-term care and public-health-emergency prescriptions; only 721.070(A)(3) points to a practitioner-held waiver under 721.075. When s. 20(c) says the seven-day written route applies where "the practitioner has received an exception from using an electronic prescription from the commissioner pursuant to subsection (h) of section 23", it is referring to that regulatory scheme, not exclusively to a personal waiver. A candidate applying decision_logic[1] to a vignette in which an ordinary prescriber telephones a Schedule IV prescription during a system outage will conclude that only the two-day electronic follow-up is available, when 105 CMR 721.070(B) gives the practitioner up to seven business days to deliver a written or electronic prescription. The framing also makes the section's own citation of 721.070(B) hard to reconcile with its decision logic.

findings.location: forms_records[0]; forms_records[1] (field has no entry for the follow-up document or its handling)
findings.problem: The section's declared subtopic is "Oral receipt, follow-up documentation, and the out-of-state oral pathway", but forms_records says nothing about what the follow-up document must contain or what the pharmacy does with it when it arrives.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires the practitioner to indicate on the electronic or written follow-up prescription that it is being issued to document an oral prescription, and then provides that "Upon receipt, the dispensing pharmacy shall attach said prescription to the oral prescription which the pharmacy has reduced to writing". 105 CMR 721.070(B) repeats the annotation requirement for the written prescription. Both are duties on the facts the section exists to teach - the pharmacist's record is incomplete until the two documents are joined - and a candidate asked what the pharmacy must do when the follow-up arrives has nothing in this section to answer with. The section also states in timing_deadlines[1] that the writing "must be postmarked within the period", which is correct under s. 20(c) and 721.070(B), so it is plainly working in this territory and has simply left the receiving-side duty out.

findings.problem: timing_deadlines[1] gives the follow-up period as "Not more than 7 days, or 7 business days under 105 CMR 721.070(B)" and never tells the candidate which measure governs, and the section omits the emergency oral Schedule II follow-up period entirely.
findings.rationale: Two problems sit here. First, seven business days is a longer period than seven calendar days, so the choice decides whether a follow-up delivered on day nine is timely; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) sets "not more than 7 days" for the written route and 105 CMR 721.070(B) sets "not more than seven business days" for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under a 721.070(A) exception. The section flags the difference in exceptions[1] but resolves nothing, and timing_deadlines[1] then presents both as one entry, leaving the candidate to guess. Second, the section's ma_vs_federal[0] and timing_deadlines[1] both assert that "a shorter federal period controls" without ever naming a federal period. The period that actually bites is the emergency oral Schedule II follow-up: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the practitioner to deliver a written prescription within 7 days, and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the Massachusetts counterpart as seven business days. A candidate cannot apply an unnamed rule, and the section's own common_traps[0] - which warns against quoting a single seven-day figure and then names only two of the periods - reinforces the impression that the list is complete.

findings.problem: The emergency oral Schedule II pathway is absent from a section whose title is "Massachusetts Oral Prescriptions and the Electronic-Prescribing Exceptions" and whose first learning objective is to carry out the pharmacist's duties when an oral controlled-substance prescription is received.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.060(B) permits a pharmacist in an Emergency Situation to dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on written or oral authorization, subject to conditions the section teaches nowhere: the quantity is limited to the amount adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period; the prescription must contain everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's actual signature and must be immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or reduced to writing; the pharmacist must make a reasonable good faith effort to establish the authorization came from a prescribing practitioner if the practitioner is not known; the practitioner must within seven business days cause an electronic or written prescription for the emergency quantity to be delivered, bearing "Authorization for Emergency Dispensing" on its face; and the dispensing pharmacist must attach it to the earlier writing and must notify the nearest DEA office if the practitioner fails to deliver. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) routes emergency-situation prescriptions into this scheme, so it is one of the electronic-prescribing exceptions the section's title claims. The DEA-notification duty in 721.060(B)(5) is a pharmacist duty of exactly the kind learning_objectives[0] promises and is a standard examination point; a candidate who studies this section will not know it exists.

findings.problem: The section's single Massachusetts-versus-federal statement asserts that "a shorter federal period controls where federal law imposes one" and no federal period is named anywhere in the section.
findings.rationale: Both M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) and 105 CMR 721.070(B) carry the qualifier "or such shorter period that is required by federal law", and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) carries it too, so the section is right that the qualifier exists. But it is a pointer, and the section never follows it. The federal period it points at is 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4), which requires the prescribing practitioner who authorized an emergency oral Schedule II prescription to cause a written prescription to be delivered to the pharmacy within 7 days - against the seven business days Massachusetts states at 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4). Because the section also omits the emergency oral Schedule II pathway entirely, a candidate has neither the trigger nor the figure, and the only Massachusetts-federal comparison the field offers cannot be performed. A study section whose subject is follow-up periods and which devotes one field to the state-federal relationship needs to name the period that actually displaces the state one.

findings.problem: The exception-route follow-up is described as a written prescription throughout, but 105 CMR 721.070(B) allows the practitioner to satisfy it with either a written or an electronic prescription.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.070(B) reads "shall, within a period of not more than seven business days, or such shorter period that is required by federal law, cause a Written or Electronic Prescription for the prescribed controlled substance to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy". Only the postmark requirement is specific to the written route. A candidate taught that the exception route is the written route may treat an electronic follow-up arriving on day five as failing to discharge the duty, or may look for a paper document that never has to exist.

results.summary: Not publishable as written. The core of the section is sound and I want to be specific about what I confirmed before the failures. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires the pharmacist on receiving an oral controlled-substance prescription to reduce it to writing immediately on a prescription form with the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the name of any expressly authorized representative, the date, the drug name, dosage and strength per dosage unit, the serial number assigned by the dispensing pharmacy, the pharmacy name, the patient's name and address, the directions for use and required cautionary statements, and the number of refills - quick_review[0] and forms_records[0] state this correctly, including the serial number, which is easy to lose. Section 20(b) requires a reasonable effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered practitioner where the prescriber is not known, and s. 20(c) does close with "The requirements of this subsection shall not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI of section 3", so exceptions[0] is right that the follow-up duty and not the receipt duty is what Schedule VI escapes. 105 CMR 721.070(C) reads exactly as quick_review[2] and common_traps[3] say it does. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) confirms the whole out-of-state limb: an authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III to VI prescription, the pharmacist must verify a Schedule III to V prescription by telephone or other means and shall not fill one for which verification cannot be obtained, the paragraph authorizes only the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and "In the case of any oral prescription for a schedule III through V substance, the pharmacist shall record that he has requested that the practitioner deliver or mail to the dispensing pharmacy a written prescription ... within seven days or such shorter period required by Federal law". The section's insistence in common_traps[1] and timing_deadlines[3] that this period runs on the practitioner's delivery and not on the pharmacist's recording is a genuinely good distinction and it is correct. The five-day out-of-state Schedule II contrast in exceptions[3] and common_traps[5] is also correct: s. 18(d) and s. 18(d 1/2) both authorize filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding five days. The section nonetheless fails, principally on the Failover. 105 CMR 721.010 defines a Failover as a document that originates as a schedule VI Electronic Prescription and is converted to a computer generated facsimile after an unforeseen transmission defect. The section never says this. Instead decision_logic[3] keys the Failover to "A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission", which is the trigger of a different provision, 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2), under which an oral prescription for a Schedule II-V controlled substance does owe a follow-up within seven business days under 721.070(B). A candidate who works decision_logic[3] on a Schedule IV telephone order taken during a system outage will satisfy all three stated conditions, conclude no follow-up is owed, and be wrong in a way that leaves a required prescriber document unrequested. That is a High defect and it drives paraphrase_fidelity, material_exceptions, actor_and_scope, decision_logic, overgeneralization and study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion. Three further failures compound it: the seven-day route is repeatedly conditioned on a prescriber who personally "holds" an exception when M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) and 105 CMR 721.070(A) make almost all of the exceptions category-based rather than practitioner-held; timing_deadlines[1] leaves "7 days" and "7 business days" side by side without saying which governs, while ma_vs_federal[0] promises that a shorter federal period controls and never names one; and the emergency oral Schedule II pathway of 105 CMR 721.060(B), including the "Authorization for Emergency Dispensing" annotation, the attachment duty and the pharmacist's duty to notify the nearest DEA office when the practitioner fails to deliver, is missing from a section that claims the electronic-prescribing exceptions in its title. forms_records also omits the s. 20(c) requirement that the follow-up indicate it documents an oral prescription and that the pharmacy attach it to the writing it made. Practice mapping is the one bright spot and it passes. All six linked questions - MA-Q-0027, MA-Q-0034, MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0123, MA-Q-0124, MA-Q-0382 - are RELEASED, and each turns on a proposition this section does teach: the 30-day out-of-state window with verification, its expiry at day 31, the s. 20(a) immediate writing with the Schedule VI carve-out from s. 20(c), the 721.070(C) no-verification rule, the out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway with the recorded request, and the paired s. 20(b) and s. 20(c) failures in MA-Q-0382, which decision_logic[1] and timing_deadlines[0] answer directly. No question depends on the defective Failover material, which is why mapping passes while the section does not.
